This kind of divides me. I am a developer and I recently loss my job. I worked as a game dev for a slot games studio, when they just decided to close the ops in europe and open new ops in Asia. They opened a new studio full of AI Slop games. Basically transitioned between quality to quantity. I think they are currently in that phase where they are blinded by the idea of more profit with less work and in the future they will need to go back because gamblers already spend too much money in this kind of games, they will want quality and immersion, not AI Slop. On our studio we were already using AI and we were starting to deliver more and more games with more and more quality, because that's what AI should be used for: to make us more powerful. I personally wasn't using it, but in spite of kind of losing my job to it, I am now in my free time developing new skills, and in fact AI does what you said: made me more powerful. It's like using a calculator in the past. You can either just use the calculator just to make quick calculations, or you can use it to not spend hours on complicated numerical calculations and instead focus more on the logic part of what whatever you are calculating. AI has been the same for me. Instead of spending hours in slack and documentation to check for best libraries to do something I can just ask it "what is the best library I can use in C# to organize validations without using giant if else blocks". I also lack knowledge on devops, but thanks to AI now I can understand how basic CI/CD pipelines work. Besides this, I believe that it should be heavy regulated, because leaving it in the hands of corporations with short sighted CEOs that just want quick profit can lead to economical disaster. In an extreme scenario, AI can massively increase productivity, but if everyone is unemployed, who will consume?
